newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan watchdog mulls deregulation of mergers.
newsitem.headline: Japan watchdog mulls deregulation of mergers.

text.p: Japan's fair trade watchdog said on Tuesday it was aiming to ease rules for mergers, which could pave the way for big corporate tie-ups and strengthen companies' global competitiveness.

Japan's strict anti-monopoly regulations have been a stumbling block for large companies seeking to boost their international competitiveness through mergers, at a time when their foreign rivals are enjoying a merger boom.
The Fair Trade Commission (FTC) said it may simplify procedures by allowing certain mergers to be conducted without the need for watchdog approval.

This would involve dropping application requirements for mergers between small firms with total assets of less than 10 billion yen ($86.9 million) each, as well as for those within the same corporate group.
"The proposed measure is in line with the government's deregulation policy," a senior FTC official told Reuters.

The quasi-governmental body said it is also looking at abolishing a guideline which stipulates that mergers of companies with combined market shares of more than 25 percent in a certain product would be examined more stringently than other mergers.
Similarly, a rule may also be dropped that requires closer scrutiny of mergers giving the combined company the biggest share of a market, if that share exceeds 15 percent.
Although the guideline does not forbid mergers which would create companies exceeding the specified market share levels, it has virtually prevented such mergers.

The new system, which the FTC is hoping to implement by late 1998, could slash the number of merger applications. About 90 percent of the 2,500 FTC applications filed in 1995/96 would had been unnecessary under the new system.
Meanwhile, U.S. corporations have been experiencing a merger boom for nearly two years, with telecommunications, utilities and insurance companies leading the way.

The driving force in the trend has been the high-flying U.S. stock market, coupled with corporate trends that stress consolidation and cost-cutting. And the consolidation trend is helping corporate America strengthen its international position.
In Japan, one of the biggest beneficiaries of the proposed deregulation is likely to be the petrochemical industry, analysts said.
Spurred by intensifying international competition, Japanese petrochemical firms have been merging production operations in order to save on capital investment and cut prices.

"The proposed deregulation needs be implemented if Japan's petrochem firms are to operate internationally and compete with their counterparts in the United States and Europe," said Masami Sawato, an analyst at BZW Research.
Sawato said that even if a Japanese petrochemical company holds more than 25 percent of the domestic market in a certain product, the scale of production is still very small in international terms.
A spokesman for Sumitomo Chemical Co Ltd, one of the largest comprehensive chemical producers in Japan, said the company welcomed the FTC move.
But the Sumitomo Chemical official also called for further deregulation to make it easier for large companies to merge.
The FTC official said the watchdog will maintain its policy of checking on mergers that might inhibit competition. ($1=115 yen)
